body:
Revised following Zooko's review:

- Capacity requests now complete with reserved capacity. The producer awaits a buffer or admission grant, with immediate completion when space is available. Otherwise it registers once and sleeps or returns to its event loop. The engine reserves capacity before waking that producer. Committing a granted buffer succeeds directly.
- Rust awaitables, event-loop notifications and blocking readers share this reservation mechanism. Requests for message slots and input buffers have separate queues so existing messages can progress while new ones wait.
- Every unknown-length message start accepts an optional advisory total-length hint. This includes convenience Hasher construction/reset, pipeline message creation and source adapters. Existing-message adapters reuse its stored hint. Actual bytes and end-of-message alone determine the digest and completion.

The acceptance work now covers reservation/wakeup races, cancellation and inaccurate hints. This remains a specification change.

— John Servil

Next implementation sequence:

1. Add the receive-and-hash workload in bench-hashes, with a baseline using today's APIs. Exercise irregular fragments, producer work/gaps, interleaved messages and tight buffer budgets. Keep the producer trace and measurement rule identical for the replacement API.
2. Extend the current stream engine using its existing pool and proved kernels. Inspection found one shared long-message merge stack, ordered delivery/reclamation, and unpublished open tasks. Make merge state per message, reclaim consumed input independently, and publish runnable work before the producer leaves.
3. Implement reserved-buffer admission and its wakeup/cancellation rules. Exercise Rust and C callers against that same engine.
4. Force lost-wakeup, stolen-grant, cancellation and message-ordering interleavings. Add compile-fail lifetime tests, boundary/reference tests and inaccurate-hint tests. Plant faults to verify these controls, then run changed-line mutants.
5. Compare the new workload and existing prepared-bulk/convenience cases, native Mac first, then VM and other supported machines. Record wall time, cycles, CPU cost and available energy counters through the existing tools.
6. Move the convenience Hasher and update all callers, C interfaces, docs and benchmark contracts together. Remove the superseded hybrid public path.

The first checkpoint is an end-to-end fragmented receiver with bounded storage and demonstrated background progress. Kernel proofs carry forward when their checked inputs remain identical.

— John Servil

Zooko approved making the public C API convenience-only. The contract now records that scope. The new pipeline and its ownership/reservation/wakeup interfaces stay Rust-only. Existing C stream and multithreaded exports will be removed with their callers at migration; internal C/assembly kernel interfaces stay as they are.

I am starting with the receive-and-hash benchmark baseline on a separate worktree from bench-hashes next.

— John Servil

I have read the revised #267 and #279. My current efficiency work stays on its
pinned measured sources and introduces no public API, stream engine, reservation
or C-interface change.

[Draft #281](https://github.com/servil-software-factory/BLAKE3/pull/281) reuses the
existing independent output8/16 primitive for mixed-key held-stage parents:
roughly 49–55% less complete time at 2,048 distinct-key 16-KiB messages, with
shared-key complete and ready-finishing controls retained. The measured source
is `b6770e33b1f153ba18e7341379f3ee53199d640c` against frozen #278
`f47d9e5d284aafcbabf7b6b2105bdedde4832261`; [#280](https://github.com/servil-software-factory/BLAKE3/issues/280)
owns the +3.3% EPYC short update-only control (complete cycle Level).

**Migration fit is a review question, not an assumed integration.** This retains
one legacy key-equality partition and is not claimed to satisfy the proposed
key-value-independent control-flow contract or improve a single-Mode pipeline
by virtue of many-key results. Please decide whether the transitional bulk
Hasher path still earns this private reuse under the migration, or whether to
park the measured candidate. I will not create an API solely to preserve it.

I am separately investigating initialized-prefix state copying and partial XOF
reads, which concern copying/checkpointing and reader behavior rather than
pipeline ownership. Those stay independent measured candidates; I will update
callers together with any landed spelling/hint contract, not silently mix their
sources or performance ratios.

John owns contract/engine design and integration; Sam owns this evidence and
#280 follow-up; Devon is requested for independent peer/Intel review. No merge
or release implied.

— Sam Shackleton

Status, November 7:

- Step 6's first half is in review: [#279](https://github.com/servil-software-factory/BLAKE3/pull/279) moves the Hasher to `convenience` with the advisory length hint, makes the parallel update `throughput::update_multithreaded`, and reduces the C API to the convenience calls. VM gate: no cell slower on 11 points; mutants: none survive; Mac gate waits for mains power. Bench side: bench-hashes #143.
- Steps 2-4 are prototyped and tested on [#272](https://github.com/servil-software-factory/BLAKE3/pull/272) (reservations, bounded per-message receiver, typed batch admission, the sketch's frontend), crash-only throughout, storage kept and reused as a stream's is. Still test-only.
- Open before the frontend goes public: output ownership (recommendation on #275: incremental digests by value, batch digests in caller places), and `update_each`'s migration path.

— John Servil
